item.title: We often think of extreme heat as simply uncomfortable, but for pregnant women the risks can be far more serious. Research has linked heat exposure to premature births. Access to…
item.description: We often think of extreme heat as simply uncomfortable, but for pregnant women the risks can be far more serious. Research has linked heat exposure to premature births. Access to shade, clean water and somewhere cool should never be a luxury. Black Lion Studios Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Secrets of the avian calendar: When do migratory birds have the opportunity to reset their schedule?
item.description: A team led by Vojtěch Brlík from Charles University in Czechia and the University of Guelph in Canada analyzed data from more than 2,300 birds tracked using miniature devices to find out how closely linked individual stages of the migratory birds' annual cycle are. The scientists were also interested in whether these linkages break down at a certain stage and whether late-departing individuals can make up for their delay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new spin on catalysts: A roadmap for smarter chemical reactions
item.description: Electron spin is a quantum property that makes electrons behave like tiny magnets. It can influence how electrons interact with each other and how chemical reactions take place. But what does this have to do with producing fertilizers, making cleaner fuels or improving energy technologies? What connects all these processes is the use of catalysts, materials that help chemical reactions happen faster and more efficiently. By controlling electron spin, scientists may be able to improve how these catalysts work, opening up new possibilities for more efficient chemical processes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lecturers and students see AI use very differently, study finds
item.description: Instructors and students have significantly different perceptions of how much generative artificial intelligence (AI) is being used in university studies, according to new research from The University of Manchester and Spain's Universidad del Pais Vasco/Euskal Herriko Unibertsitatea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild animals can now GPS-collar themselves for research
item.description: For six decades, wildlife researchers have faced a persistent challenge: to attach a tracking device to study a wild animal, they first have to catch it. Now, a new approach developed at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences (NMBU) allows GPS collars to be deployed autonomously on free-roaming terrestrial wildlife. Published in BioScience, the proof-of-concept study demonstrates Capture-Free Telemetry (CFT), a technique that places tracking devices on wild animals as they interact with baited deployment units in their natural habitat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Millions of bogong moths are blanketing cities in Australia, and they are still endangered
item.description: In recent weeks, people across Australia have found fluttering bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) in their homes, cars and even bedrooms. These insects have embarked on their annual migration from breeding grounds across southern Australia to the cool caves of the Australian Alps. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seagrass helps Biscayne Bay's mangroves keep up with rising seas
item.description: The mangroves of Biscayne Bay have been getting help from an unlikely neighbor—the seagrass meadows just offshore. Dead seagrass blades and seaweed drift loose until the tide carries them into the mangroves, where they pile up, rot slowly and then become part of the ground. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study reveals how five tuna species respond to changing Mediterranean conditions
item.description: As the Mediterranean Sea continues to warm, it may become more favorable for some tropical tuna species. However, warmer waters do not necessarily provide all the environmental conditions these highly migratory fish need. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: CT scans reveal four-letter code to 400-year-old lock from Welsh shipwreck
item.description: Experts from Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University have used cutting-edge CT scanning technology to unlock a centuries-old combination lock recovered from one of Wales' most remarkable maritime discoveries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smiling can make you happier—unless someone forces you to do it
item.description: Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., had long heard that forcing a smile can make you feel a little happier—after all, he had done a lot of the research that supposedly proved it. But something didn't sit quite right with his own findings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists develop novel model to forecast internal solitary waves from multiple sources in the Sulu Sea
item.description: A research team led by Professor Li Xiaofeng from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS) has developed a model to forecast internal solitary waves originating from multiple sources in the Sulu Sea. The model combines physical equations and satellite observations to predict wave arrival times and crest positions across this complex marine environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Does opting out of TV tracking work?
item.description: The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn't new, but what and how they're tracking - and if we can stop it - is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works. While opting out was […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: John Higgins

item.title: Tiny melt traces shed light on the Colorado Plateau's explosive past
item.description: Deep beneath Earth's surface, some minerals hold clues to processes that happened millions of years ago. One such mineral is lawsonite, which forms under high pressure and relatively low temperatures. What makes it significant is its ability to store water within its crystal structure and carry it deep into Earth as tectonic plates move beneath one another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Limited cold stress during pregnancy could lead to increased lamb birth weight, survivability
item.description: Research out of South Dakota State University has highlighted a potential connection between limited exposure to cold stress during pregnancy and birth weight. The work showed that shearing ewes at day 50 of gestation, rather than after 100 days, resulted in larger and heavier lambs at birth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
item.description: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
item.description: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why AI influencers work better with a human friend
item.description: Scroll through Instagram long enough and you'll meet an influencer who isn't real. AI influencers—computer-generated personalities like Lil Miquela, who has millions of followers and has posted for Prada, Samsung and Dior—look and act like human creators, but they're entirely synthetic. Brands like them because they never go off-script, never age and never cause a scandal. Yet they share one stubborn weakness: people tend not to trust them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
item.description: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How to say 'no' to your child—and stick to it
item.description: "No" may be one of the hardest words for parents to say to a young child. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a simple mechanical squeeze can dramatically alter the magnetic properties and electrical behavior of exotic materials called altermagnets. The surprising breakthrough could open the door to faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
item.description: MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Research reveals accelerating sea-level rise around Ireland
item.description: A new study led by the ICARUS Climate Research Center at Maynooth University in Ireland has reconstructed a century of Irish sea-level change, revealing a stark acceleration in sea-level rise. The research, titled "A Century of Sea-Level Change in Ireland (1925–2024)" and published in Ocean Science, combines tide-gauge records from six locations, including newly digitized historical records from Cork, Tarbert and Galway. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: "Todavía hoy me arrepiento": Spielberg aún se lamenta del impacto causado por esta obra maestra que puedes recuperar en streaming
item.description: En 2022, en el programa ‘Desert Island Discs’ de BBC Radio 4: Spielberg confesaba que todavía hoy lamenta la matanza de escualos que siguió a la publicación del libro de Peter Benchley y de su popularísima adaptación ' Tiburón ' (que puedes recatar en Movistar Plus y SkyShowtime ). "Lo lamento de verdad, sinceramente", dijo. Habló además de un temor peculiar: que los tiburones sigan enfadados con él por la fiebre de pesca deportiva que se desató a partir de 1975. Un estudio publicado en Nature en 2021 le quita buena parte del peso de encima: la abundancia de tiburones y rayas oceánicos ha… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: John Tones

item.title: Enjoyment increases consumers' willingness to pay for sustainable products
item.description: Consumers are more willing to pay for sustainable products if they also perceive them as enjoyable and appealing, according to a study conducted at the University of Eastern Finland. However, environmental friendliness alone does not always translate into willingness to pay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Call adjustments help bats keep their echolocation signals distinct, study finds
item.description: Bats can produce ultrasonic pulses with high frequencies between 20,000 and 120,000 hertz, which are inaudible to humans. The sound waves they produce travel forward, hitting nearby objects and bouncing back in the form of echoes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extreme heat is becoming a fact of life in more parts of the world, with serious implications for pregnant women and their babies.... Ver más
item.description: Extreme heat is becoming a fact of life in more parts of the world, with serious implications for pregnant women and their babies.... Ver más We often think of extreme heat as simply uncomfortable, but for pregnant women the risks can be far more serious. Research has linked heat exposure to premature births. Access to shade, clean water and somewhere cool should never be a luxury. Tenemos… Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
item.description: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
item.description: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Por increíble que parezca, hay gente comprando cadáveres de hace siglos en Facebook
item.description: En Facebook e Instagram se anuncian cabezas, manos y otros restos de cuerpos humanos a precios competitivos. Son piezas momificadas de hace siglos que se ofertan como si fueran objetos de segunda mano. Sin embargo, lo que parece una extravagancia macabra esconde un negocio internacional que los investigadores llevan años siguiendo. Y han encontrado algo más inquietante que cualquier maldición egipcia: unos hongos potencialmente peligrosos, sustancias tóxicas y restos humanos que viajan por correo hasta las casas de sus compradores. Momias a golpe de clic. Un estudio titulado The Real Mummy’s… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: Toxic air pollution surges in Indian capital
item.description: Toxic air pollution in India's capital, New Delhi, surged on Wednesday to more than 30 times the World Health Organization's recommended daily limit, data from air monitors showed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study calls for a rethink on how we manage the threats posed by hazardous species
item.description: While human well-being depends on the health of our ecosystems, there are also countless aspects of the natural world that pose serious threats to people. Every year, over 700,000 people die from diseases transmitted by animals, snakebites kill up to 500,000 people, and crop loss from pests carries an estimated cost of around $220 billion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Six measures could save 1.6 million lives a year: WHO
item.description: Implementing a few climate and health measures could save nearly 1.6 million lives a year and generate trillions of dollars for the economy, the World Health Organization said Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Time to wake up MetOp-SG-B1 weather satellite
item.description: Following a short period in storage after arriving at Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana, the MetOp Second Generation-B1 satellite has been transferred to a cleanroom and removed from its transport container. The team is now preparing to reactivate this ‘sleeping beauty, and begin the final checks and preparations ahead of its launch, planned towards the end of the year. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La Antártida esconde un secreto bajo sus suelos helados: el 91 % de las cepas de una bacteria analizada solo aparece allí
item.description: La Antártida se ve como un paraje donde solo se pueden encontrar pingüinos, pero la realidad es que también es una tierra que puede llegar a fascinar a cualquier microbiólogo por la adaptación que han sufrido diferentes bacterias. Tal es así que un nuevo análisis genético a gran escala hecho sobre los suelos de la Antártida ha demostrado que el continente helado tiene sus propias reglas, puesto que la inmensa mayoría de las cepas de un género bacteriano muy común en todo el mundo resulta ser endémico de estas tierras. El estudio. Ha sido publicado recientemente en la revista PNAS, y aporta… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Before the Dawn in America’s Heartland
item.description: With hardly a cloud in sight, astronauts had a sweeping view of nighttime lights in the U.S. Midwest. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Testing Einstein's laws from the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea
item.description: Are the laws of physics truly the same everywhere in the universe? This fundamental principle, known as Lorentz invariance, lies at the heart of Einstein's theory of relativity. Yet some theories that seek to reconcile gravity with quantum physics suggest that it might not always hold. To investigate this possibility, researchers from the international KM3NeT collaboration analyzed 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events detected by KM3NeT/ORCA, a neutrino telescope located deep in the Mediterranean Sea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Loophole listing keeps seafood qualifying as critically endangered on the menu
item.description: One of Australia's most dangerously overfished species, redfish (Centroberyx affinis), will continue to be served on our dinner tables following its latest listing as "conservation dependent." The classification is a loophole allowing species that qualify for critically endangered listings and protections to instead be killed and sold for seafood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A vampire burial: A Polish woman was buried with a sickle to stop her rising from the grave
item.description: Unveiled by time, Zosia's grave in Pień offers a glimpse into 17th century Polish traditions regarding death and the supernatural. Archaeologists found an iron sickle and a toe-bound padlock alongside her remains, suggesting efforts to prevent her from rising as a vampire. This peculiar burial practice hints at Zosia's affluent background, compelling researchers to dive deeper into her life and the cultural fears that shaped her final resting place. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
item.description: A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
item.description: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Who killed British archaeologist James Starkey? Archival records shed light on an 88-year-old mystery
item.description: Eighty-eight years after pioneering British archaeologist Starkey was shot dead while traveling from the ancient city of Lachish to Jerusalem, researchers say they have uncovered compelling new evidence explaining who was behind his murder—and why he was targeted. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
item.description: Article URL: https://www.dana-farber.org/newsroom/news-releases/2026/study-reveals-distinct-cellular-and-genetic-differences-in-colorectal-cancer-in-younger-patients Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50361154 Points: 99 # Comments: 38 Fuente: Hacker News - Portada.
item.dc:creator: gmays

item.title: Researchers develop sensors for continuous corn growth monitoring
item.description: When is the best time to apply nitrogen? What plant response was there to fertilizer or any number of other treatments? There is a general answer to those questions now, but what if plant breeders and agronomists could download data from continuously monitored cornstalks and ears to develop specific answers for those questions? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
item.description: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: One in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse, study finds
item.description: Around one in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse, according to a new study. The general-population survey of more than 7,200 adults in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia found 7% had experienced at least one form of AI-generated image-based abuse since turning 18. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Want more social media engagement? Research suggests changing the message, not your personality
item.description: Want more engagement on social media? Stop repeating yourself. Just don't change who you are in the process. That's according to new Case Western Reserve University research suggesting that public figures can increase engagement by varying their topics and wording while "maintaining a consistent psychological voice." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese scientists discover thickening ground ice in parts of warming Tibet
item.description: The Tibetan Plateau, home to the world’s largest expanse of alpine permafrost, is warming at about twice the global average but, counter-intuitively,researchers have found that ice in parts of the Tibet autonomous region is actually thickening. A team from Peking University found that shallow ground ice has unexpectedly increased over the past 20 years, affecting more than a third of the plateau’s permafrost, a phenomenon driven largely by natural climate factors. The authors noted that the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Dannie Peng

item.title: Lab-grown neurons retain features of embryonic development
item.description: Scientists from Skoltech, together with colleagues from the Kharkevich Institute for Information Transmission Problems of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Lomonosov Moscow State University and other organizations, conducted a comparative study of the 3D genome organization in neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells and in neurons of the adult human brain. The authors collected and processed more than 300 3D genome maps covering 62 human samples and 34 mouse samples, including data on embryonic stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, neural progenitors, fetal and postmortem… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shared data ecosystem could help scientists explore new biological connections
item.description: Scientists generate vast amounts of research data, but connecting information across studies can be difficult. The NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem is working to change that by making research data sets from 18 NIH programs easier to find, connect and analyze. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Digitalization front-runners are more vulnerable to cyberattacks
item.description: For many business leaders, digitalization is associated with promises of greater efficiency and productivity. However, a new study by professor of accounting Jukka Sihvonen from the University of Vaasa, Finland, suggests that increasing digitalization may also raise a company's risk of falling victim to a successful cyberattack. The study has been published in the journal British Journal of Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
item.description: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study maps Nelore cattle microbiota to reduce methane emissions
item.description: Researchers at the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (EMBRAPA) are studying the relationship between the genetics of Nelore cattle and the microorganisms in their guts (microbiota). Nelore cattle are the most widely raised beef breed in Brazil. The goal is to develop strategies that reduce emissions of methane—a major greenhouse gas—and improve the animals' feed efficiency. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El recuerdo de Cristina Koch, primera mujer en viajar a la Luna, sobre la misión: “Veíamos destellos azules cuando cerrábamos los ojos”
item.description: Tras completar con éxito el histórico sobrevuelo lunar, se conoció una frase que la astronauta de la NASA pronunció mientras realizaba la misión Artemis II Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: North Atlantic's 'cold blob' may contain climate nuance
item.description: Climate observers have long tied the strength of a major ocean current to water temperatures in the so-called "cold blob" in the North Atlantic Ocean. The 965,000-square-mile (2.5 million square kilometers) area south and southeast of Greenland cooled by as much as 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit over the past century as other ocean waters warmed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How the nasal microbiome can help potentially harmful bacteria thrive
item.description: Our noses are home to many different species of bacteria living side by side. One of them may be S. aureus. Many people carry this bacterium without knowing it, although it can cause serious infections. Why S. aureus colonizes some people persistently but not others remains only partly understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Semiautomated platform delivers consistent batches of extracellular vesicles for potential regenerative therapies
item.description: A study led by researchers from the Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP) and the Blood and Tissue Bank (BST) has developed and validated a manufacturing platform for extracellular vesicles that meets pharmaceutical quality requirements, marking a key step toward their clinical application. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using vibrations to reveal what lies beneath other planets' surfaces
item.description: Modern space exploration hasn't quite reached "Star Trek" levels of boldly going where no one has gone before. But if, like the denizens of the USS Enterprise, astronauts one day want to land on an uncharted planet, they'd first want to know what's on—and under—the surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny fossils show brittle stars gathered around a dead whale 9.5 million years ago
item.description: Tiny skeletal plates recovered beside fossil whale bones in southern Denmark offer a rare glimpse of life around a whale carcass approximately 9.5 million years ago. Researchers have identified a new species of brittle star, Ophiura huebnerjenseni, from the Gram Clay Pit and suggest it represents the first fossil record of brittle stars associated with a whale fall. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Disillusion runs deep among young Americans, poll reveals
item.description: The kids are not all right on the future. For the first time in the 26-year history of the Harvard Youth Poll, more respondents expect to be worse off financially than their parents (27%) than better off (25%). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03544-8 It might seem counterproductive to put more people in nature, but sometimes human activity nurtures biodiversity. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03168-y Neuroscientists are developing a new type of brain implant that will decode every movement and symptom of people with this neurodegenerative condition, seeking better ways to ease symptoms. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03580-4 The latest cases, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, come as the country grapples with ongoing Ebola and cholera outbreaks. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03505-1 For decades, conservation has worried about the risks of too many people. In some places, depopulation is the real threat. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Emma Marris

item.title: Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03170-4 Researchers and advocates point to pollutants as a trigger for the neurodegenerative condition. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Tammy Worth

item.title: Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03166-0 After decades of work, researchers have begun trialling transplants of dopamine neurons into people with the neurodegenerative disease — with early signs of success. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Laura Dattaro

item.title: Southern Ocean waters reveal distinct nutrient recycling pathways during decades-long journeys north
item.description: The Southern Ocean may seem far removed from the North Pacific or the Gulf of Maine, but its waters are linked to all the world's major ocean basins through a vast circulation system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Asymmetric atomic structure improves sodium–sulfur battery performance
item.description: Chinese researchers have developed a new way to improve sodium–sulfur battery performance by changing the atomic structure of a catalyst. Led by professors Wang Hui and Zheng Fangcai from the High Magnetic Field Laboratory at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the study is published in Angewandte Chemie. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Finding the fingerprints of noisy distributions in random quantum systems
item.description: Imagine shuffling a deck of cards where some of the cards are fading just because of the way they interact with the external environment as you shuffle them. Your job is to figure out the interplay between the shuffling, or "imposed randomness," due to the way you shuffle your cards and how that relates to the fading as cards are exposed to the external environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tijuana River pollution doesn't stay put—it can travel seven times farther than expected
item.description: Waste dumped into the Tijuana River can travel seven times farther than expected before becoming airborne and affecting San Diego's air, at least 20 miles (32 kilometers) from its source, according to new UC Riverside research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New framework helps turn biodiversity goals into measurable action
item.description: The new study by Newcastle University and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) offers a practical roadmap for tracking progress toward halting species extinctions by 2050. It guides users from understanding where species are most at risk in a given area, through taking action to reduce species threats, to measuring the real-world impact of conservation efforts on reducing species extinction risk over time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Body size, not competition, may kick-start evolution
item.description: A new evolutionary theory suggests changes in body size, rather than competition for food and habitat, may drive the earliest physical differences between species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Talk of the town: Virtual world gets stroke survivors talking
item.description: Have you ever felt like you know exactly what you want to say, but just can't get the words out? Having a word on the tip of your tongue can be frustrating at the best of times, but for people with communication difficulties, it can be a constant struggle to find the right words, make sentences and connect with others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scarcer food may have pushed early humans to rework stone tools for longer use
item.description: About 300,000 years ago, the emergence of the first Homo sapiens in Africa was accompanied by major cultural and technological changes, marking the beginning of a new archaeological period, the Middle Stone Age. At that time, African landscapes were also undergoing profound transformations. To understand how the earliest members of our species lived and adapted, it is therefore essential to reconstruct the environments in which they lived. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When should we listen for alien signals? Scientists turn to game theory
item.description: Finding a signal from an extraterrestrial civilization takes more than just pointing a telescope in the right direction. We may also need to listen at exactly the right time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stone Age hunters in northern Europe may have used poison arrows to hunt big prey
item.description: Autumn walks in Britain are glorious, as the foliage changes color and cool, crisp air begins to bite. However, some of these European trees hide a much darker secret. For example, the yew tree's lovely red arils—the cup-shaped coverings around the seeds—carry toxins that may have been used to poison arrow tips in the past. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How humans influence fish behavior and why this is important for species conservation
item.description: Two recent review articles in the journals Trends in Ecology & Evolution and Fish and Fisheries, to which researchers from the Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) contributed, focus on the influence of humans on the diversity of fish behavior and on how management can help preserve this diversity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Single-copy genes can be used as markers to distinguish between bacteria in the same family
item.description: The more than 100 bacterial species of the genus Vibrio are important in marine ecosystems because they contribute to the carbon cycle and other ecological processes, but they can also be significant pathogens for both humans (they can cause cholera) and animals (they can drastically reduce productivity in fish and crustacean farms [e.g., prawns] or cause coral bleaching). Identifying and quantifying Vibrio species in marine and estuarine water samples is complex because identification errors may occur when using molecular methods that lack sufficient resolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers develop method for single-cell DNA methylation analysis
item.description: Researchers have recently developed a standardized workflow for analyzing DNA methylation in individual cells. The protocol combines an improved laboratory procedure with an automated data analysis tool, making it easier to study differences between cells. Published in Nature Protocols, the study was led by researchers from the Institute of Health and Medical Technology at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The marginalia found in millions of Arabic manuscripts could reshape our understanding of Islamic history
item.description: For a comprehensive understanding of the content of millions of Arabic manuscripts held in libraries around the world, it is crucial for scholars to first examine what their marginalia reveal, according to a new study published in the Journal of Islamic Thought and Civilization. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds stronger trade secret protection leads firms to break down innovation silos
item.description: To guard proprietary know-how, many firms separate their inventors into independent groups so that no single employee sees too much of the organization's knowledge. New research published in Strategic Management Journal finds that when U.S. states strengthened trade secret law, high-tech firms relied less on this kind of compartmentalization and connected their inventors more broadly—and the inventions that followed had greater technological impact. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A laser can draw superconductivity at the nanoscale
item.description: Researchers from ICMAB-CSIC, the Politecnico di Milano and Université de Liège have adapted a direct laser writing technique that allows them to "draw" superconducting properties in a material. The result is a new way to locally program the behavior of a superconductor, tuning it from a fully superconducting state to an insulating one with extraordinary precision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plant-inspired natural coatings can beat forever chemicals
item.description: Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are known as "forever chemicals" because of the impact they make on the environment and human bodies. Much of modern manufacturing relies on these substances for safe packaging, fire protection and waterproof coatings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cold storage can extend shelf life of platelets for dogs facing life-threatening bleeding
item.description: Veterinarians often have limited access to one of the most effective tools for controlling life-threatening bleeding complications in dogs: platelets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hiding inside Palantir’s skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal
item.description: Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Julie Bort

item.title: US astronauts vote from space in 2026 midterm elections
item.description: NASA astronaut Anil Menon demonstrated on social media how he cast his ballot for Harris County in Texas, from space. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
item.description: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades, according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More power, less payoff: Study reveals a bottleneck in cleaner methanol production
item.description: Dialing up the power on electricity-driven chemical reactions doesn't guarantee that they'll be more efficient, suggests a new study, a finding that gets researchers closer to creating the ideal conditions for sustainable chemical manufacturing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A single measurement makes quantum bits more reliable
item.description: Researchers at the University of Regensburg and their international partners have found a way to significantly reduce errors in quantum bits. In an experiment, they demonstrated that a single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations can cut the error rate by more than half. The results have been published in Applied Physics Reviews. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wherever there are people, there is also wildlife—though not necessarily at the same time
item.description: Human-induced global change has reached an unprecedented scale and intensity. Through intensive land use and the associated loss of species, humans are permanently altering the habitats and communities of wild animals. "How do predators manage to find their way in landscapes heavily shaped by humans and establish their niche? It is precisely this question that interested us," says Kathi Kasper, a doctoral student at the MRI PAS, the EBD-CSIC and the Leibniz-IZW and an author of the study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As it gets harder to figure out what to eat, some Americans are turning to religion for answers
item.description: It's getting harder and harder to figure out what to eat. A scroll through social media raises many questions. Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein? What about fiber? Do I need supplements? Should I be making all my bread at home? What foods were recalled this week? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reading single vesicles reveals clues to the origin of chronic inflammation
item.description: A new technique to diagnose chronic inflammation developed at Nagoya University can read information from the surface and within individual extracellular vesicles in blood and urine. This technique could be used to develop noninvasive tests that can not only detect chronic inflammation but also provide information about the tissues where it occurs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers target PFAS with lower-temperature destruction method
item.description: Removing harmful chemicals from contaminated water is only one step toward their elimination. Once collected in filtration materials, these chemicals must still be destroyed and detoxified to prevent contamination from moving into another waste stream. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global accounting reveals economic toll of ecosystem losses from rising seas
item.description: A global accounting puts the value of ecosystem services that could be lost to sea level rise at well over 100 billion in 2020 international dollars (Int$2020) per year by 2100, according to a study—and the nations that are likely to lose the most are not the highest emitters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
item.description: Cybersecurity experts have long warned of the persistent and patient threat from North Korea's long-running hacks. The world's largest crypto exchange was still caught off-guard. Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Zack Whittaker

item.title: Silent lakes ahead? Long-term study finds common loon productivity is dropping across North America
item.description: The eerie call of the common loon has long been the sound of North America's northern lakes, but new research shows it may not be that way in the future. A new study led by Birds Canada analyzed breeding attempts across nine Canadian provinces and seven U.S. states. The researchers found a widespread, long-term plunge in loon chick production across their range. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Microbiome research reveals how bacterial lipids influence liver and muscle health in mice
item.description: An interdisciplinary team of researchers from UConn and the University of Pittsburgh is filling knowledge gaps about the surprising roles that our microbiomes play in our health. The team's recent studies, published in Gastro Hep Advances and The Journal of Physiology, focus on Bacteroidota species that grow in our guts and mouths, where they produce glycine lipids that interact with our metabolism. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The shape really does read like a cat sitting with its back turned — a great reminder of how much detail Webb captures in a single frame. Realtabs Source Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Not surprising at all. I was paying too much attention to stressful and negative-tone videos, and I found myself thinking/feeling more negative. I didn’t like it, so I changed my…
item.description: Not surprising at all. I was paying too much attention to stressful and negative-tone videos, and I found myself thinking/feeling more negative. I didn’t like it, so I changed my algorithm by skipping that stuff. Much better! Laura Walsh Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Scientists revive decades-old approach to target cancer-linked genes using synthetic DNA
item.description: Researchers have developed a new approach that uses synthetic DNA molecules to target cancer-linked genes directly, opening new possibilities for future treatments, diagnostics and biological research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Double mutualist' birds are key to mistletoe reproduction
item.description: Some bird species act as "double mutualists" for a common mistletoe, both pollinating its flowers and dispersing its seeds. These double mutualists play an effective role in mistletoe reproduction. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are Counter-Strike players better at decision-making? Study reveals faster brain processing in expert gamers
item.description: Expert Counter-Strike players could make ideal candidates for fast-paced emergency service response jobs requiring split-second decision-making, according to a new University of Sheffield study aiming to debunk myths about video games. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tell this AI what you want a protein to do—and it designs one
item.description: In a short space of time, artificial intelligence has become a whiz at designing proteins, molecular machines that perform various functions such as speeding up reactions, producing fluorescent signals and breaking down plastic. But getting AI to design the specific protein you want usually requires the user to have a strong understanding of molecular structures and geometric constraints to guide the models correctly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI is changing what's in store for new hires and managers alike
item.description: AI is screening résumés, prompting some managers to hire fewer entry-level workers and leading others to expect beginners to tackle more advanced work, Northeastern University's AI & Society Survey found. The report is the latest in a series that opened with an analysis of how people across the political spectrum view AI training. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plants' immune memory hints at new crop breeding approach
item.description: A study published in Nature Communications, led by professor Jurriaan Ton and Dr. Adam Hannan Parker at the University of Sheffield, has identified mechanisms by which plants maintain and reset stress memory from past infections. This immune memory enables plants to defend themselves more effectively against harmful bacteria and mildews, which are increasingly threatening our crop and food production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unos científicos italianos viajaron a Etiopía a estudiar monos y volvieron con una inverosímil historia de amor entre un burro y un toro
item.description: En un pasto comunal de Debre Libanos, en las tierras altas de Etiopía, un burro llamado Patroclo busca a un toro llamado Achille en mitad del prado. Se le acerca y le toca con el hocico en el costado. Pasan cosas, aparecen terceros en discordia. Hay peleas, algún mordisco. Pero al final, juntos otra vez, el toro monta al asno y se queda lamiéndolo. Pero esa escena, grabada en vídeo con otras tantas, no era un hecho aislado. Lo que los investigadores italianos acaban de encontrar es una relación que desafía lo que sabemos sobre conducta animal : dos machos de familias distintas que, con vacas… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Javier Jiménez

item.title: A new way to navigate tough land and water use decisions
item.description: An open-source software tool to help find a sweet spot between competing environmental and development demands has been launched by researchers at the University of Queensland. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Boat burial reveals leprosy strain in fifth-century Germany
item.description: Visigothic and Vandal forces marched into Italy and conquered Rome; the Huns spread fear and terror on their campaigns through Western Europe; the Franks expanded their domain southward—the fifth century was an era of profound, often violent upheavals in Europe, and at the same time one of great mobility. Researchers from the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Christian-Albrechts-University in Kiel and the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research (NIhK) have now identified a specific example of this mobility in the Fallward burial ground in what is now the… Fuente: Phys.org.
